### Factors affecting teachers’ use of digital resources for teaching mathematical cultures: An extended UTAUT‑2 model

**Jinhai Liu1,2**[ ** ·**](http://orcid.org/0009-0004-6187-3750) **Qin Dai1 · Jihe Chen3**[ ](http://orcid.org/0000-0002-9650-5163)

Received: 22 May 2024 / Accepted: 3 October 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024

## Abstract Technology integration into education is a significant development that has facili- tated using digital resources in teaching mathematical culture (TMC). Despite the potential benefits, there are currently limited reports on factors influencing teachers’ use of these resources for instructional purposes. Therefore, this study aims to deter- mine the influence of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) on teachers’ behavioral intention and usage behavior towards digital resources in TMC. The study procedures were carried out based on the revised Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT-2) model. A quantitative analysis and an online survey were conducted with 418 mathematics teachers from three provinces in central and western China. The data obtained were then analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that (1) performance expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit sig- nificantly influenced teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources, and (2) behavioral intention as a mediator significantly promoted usage behavior with facili- tating conditions, habit, and TPACK having similar effects. These results have man- agerial and practical implications for scholars, teachers, school principals, and pol- icy-makers who advocate for integrating digital resources in educational contexts.

**Keywords** Digital resources · Mathematics teachers · Teaching mathematical culture · TPACK · PLS-SEM · UTAUT-2 model

## 1 Introduction

The application of digital technologies in education is a significant development that has attracted wide attention from schools and society. These technologies offer various high-quality learning resources in the form of e-textbooks, online interactive feedback, and micro-videos, adding more opportunities for knowledge exchange and

innovation (Wijaya et al., 2022b). As implementers of teaching programs, teachers have been reported to play an essential role through digital competence in educa- tion and training. In addition, their ability to adopt these technologies promotes stu- dents’ learning experience and development. Several studies also reported that the effectiveness of students’ learning is largely dependent on the information and com- munications technology (ICT) competence of teachers (George & Sanders, 2017). The UNESCO-published _ICT Competency Framework for Teachers_ provides guide- lines for training educators from K-12 to higher education, outlining essential digital skills, roles, and skillsets needed for digital education (UNESCO, 2022). Various countries have adopted ICT competency frameworks that are applicable across vari- ous education levels and teaching contexts (Tondeur et al., 2017). Concurrently, con- temporary education, facilitated by globalization, faces the challenges of meeting the needs of increasingly diverse students and instilling intercultural awareness and communication skills (Ganesan & Morales, 2024). Based on previous results, there is a growing emphasis on the integration of subject knowledge and culture in the current reform of mathematics education. In addition, incorporating the mathemati- cal and cultural context of knowledge in teaching and learning provides a platform for realizing the goal of teaching mathematical culture (TMC) (Quan & Gu, 2018). According to several reports, digital resources empower teachers to present con- tent clearly and offer students diverse scenarios of mathematical practices and appli- cations (Vahey et al., 2020). Compared to other subjects, mathematical knowledge tends to be more abstract and logical. In addition, mathematics teaching with tech- nologies provides a three-dimensional, intuitive approach, which attracts students’ attention (Chen et  al., 2021). Previous studies also showed that digital resources could facilitate the provision of personalized instruction based on students’ levels and interests, thereby enhancing learning and exploration in the mathematics class- room (Confrey et al., 2017). Recent reports have generally focused on the relation- ship between digital resources and instructional practices, such as explaining the nature of teachers’ classroom practices and technologies (Clark-Wilson et al., 2020). The use of technologies to develop technological pedagogical knowledge for pre- service mathematics teachers has been explored (Rocha, 2020). Despite the widely recognized potential of digital resources in mathematics education, their adoption by teachers in TMC is affected by complex factors (Pepin et al., 2017b). Existing studies indicate that teachers’ attitudes (Trujillo-Torres et al., 2020), technological competence (Yeo et  al., 2022), teaching beliefs (Gleisner Villasmil et  al., 2023), as well as support and pressure from the school and social environments (Lane & McAndrew, 2010), significantly influence their willingness and behavior to use digi- tal resources.

In line with previous studies, the integration of digital resources to support TMC is becoming increasingly essential (Cevikbas et al., 2023). Mathematics teachers’ intentions to adopt technologies are important in determining their adoption behav- ior and effectiveness. However, there are currently limited reports on the factors that influence the use of digital resources for TMC. The potential facilitating effect of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) skills on willingness to use digital resources is also underexplored. This shows that exploring the factors in depth and analyzing teachers’ motivations and barriers is important for promoting 

the effective application of technologies in education as well as the development of innovative thinking. This study used the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT-2) model developed by (Venkatesh et al., 2012) to identify the factors affecting mathematics teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC. The spe- cific research questions are as follows:

- What factors influence teachers’ behavioral intentions to use digital resources in TMC?
- What are the significant positive factors that have the greatest impact on teach- ers’ behavioral intentions based on the use of digital resources in TMC?
- What factors influence teachers’ usage behavior of digital resources in TMC?
- What are the most significant positive factors influencing teachers’ use behavior based on the use of digital resources in TMC?

Through systematic analysis and discussion of these factors, we can uncover the intentions and behaviors that influence mathematics teachers’ use of digi- tal resources, thereby offering both theoretical support and practical guidance to improve their effectiveness in using digital resources for TMC.

## 2 Literature review and theoretical framework

### 2.1 Digital resources in education

Digital resources are instructional materials that can be operated on a computer or in a networked environment, including multimedia software, digital images, digi- tal audio, websites, databases, data files, e-mail, and online learning systems (Fox, 2015). The emergence of these materials has caused a shift from traditional static, unresponsive print-based resources to dynamically responsive data-based resources (Pepin et  al., 2017a). In addition, the term “digital resources” is widely used in the field of education to describe specific knowledge and skills related to the pro- fessional competencies of teachers (Heine et al., 2023). Since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic globally, online digital resources have become the mainstream mode of education (Li & Liang, 2023). The use of these materials in education and the ability of teachers to handle them are increasingly becoming a hot topic of inves- tigation in various countries. For example, 70% of teachers in Germany have created digital resources for their courses (Mußmann et al., 2021). In the Australian curricu- lum, educators need to introduce these materials for teaching (Kervin et al., 2019) through (1) devices (e.g., tablets, laptops, and electronic whiteboards), (2) digital applications (‘apps’), and (3) dedicated classroom spaces (e.g., a desktop computer, an iPad station with earphones, or a Computer Lab). According to the European Framework for the Digital Competence of Educators (DigCompEdu) (Redecker & Punie, 2017), teachers often require the ability to select, create, modify, manage, protect, and share digital resources.

Several studies have shown that individuals can build a strong foundation for their teaching when open to new technologies and continually scrutinize feelings 

and attitudes in the process (Leung & Hue, 2017). The use of digital resources in education undoubtedly provides important support and assistance to teachers in cur- riculum development and subject teaching.

### 2.2 TMC supported by digital resources

TMC refers to the teaching of aspects related to the subject of mathematics that are defined as major components. For example, particular attitudes towards beauty, rigor, and simplicity are seen as attitudes, behaviors, and values that students are expected to acquire in the process of becoming mathematicians (Lei et al., 2022). Burton (Burton, 2009) stated that for mathematics to achieve widespread popu- larity, the issue of mathematical culture must be considered. Typically, traditional teaching tends to make students memorize the conclusions without exploring the ideas hidden in the formulas, which is not conducive to further learning (Hodge & Cobb, 2019). To overcome the challenge, mathematics education has incorporated the use of digital technology since the 1980s (Papert, 1982). Expressive media for mathematics education provide dynamic manipulations, interconnected represen- tations, and simulations of phenomena and situations embedded in mathematical rules, such as GeoGebra (Wu & Liu, 2023) and Hawgent Dynamic Math software (Chen et al., 2021). These media also enable knowledge construction through crea- tive engagement with (advanced) concepts (Kynigos & Kolovou, 2018). The use of dynamic software to present the process of proving mathematical formulas enhances students’ learning and allows movement from a static to a dynamic understand- ing (Chen et al., 2021). In the last two decades, the range of digital technologies available has expanded considerably. The ability of these technologies to provide students with activities that enhance learning has also increased (Bray & Tangney, 2017). Technologized mathematics activities help students from in action-cognition transduction to inform the design of specific interventions. In a test of understanding similarities, directed embodied activity produced greater learning gains than math- ematically comparable non-embodied activity (Abrahamson et al., [2020)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education). In line with previous studies, mathematical culture is the embodiment of the val- ues of mathematics to unify the spirit of mathematicians (Löwe et al., 2021). Sev- eral reports showed that TMC can improve the status quo of mathematics class- room teaching. In addition, the integration of mathematical technology and culture is conducive to enhancing students’ attention and interest in traditional culture and improving the efficiency of classroom and learning effect (Wu & Liu, 2023). The use of digital technology to develop vivid and interesting teaching materials is one of the current study priorities. The combination of digital tools with sound peda- gogy has been recognized as having the potential to promote the development of several generic learner skills, such as critical thinking and problem-solving (Viberg & Mavroudi, 2018). Among all the factors influencing students’ activity, teachers have the greatest impact on learning (Kieran et  al., 2013). Attention to teachers’ willingness to use digital technology and other variables is a current study priority (Viberg et al., 2023).

### 2.3 Unified theory of acceptance and use of technology

The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model was developed by Venkatesh et al. (Venkatesh et al., 2003) by reviewing and integrating eight dominant theories and models, i.e., The Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA) (Fishbein & Ajzen, 1975), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) (Davis & Davis, 1989), Motivational Model (MM) (Bagozzi et al., 1992), Theory of Planned Behav- ior (TPB) (Ajzen, [1991)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education), Combined TAM and TPB (C-TAM-TPB) (Taylor & Todd, 1995), Model of PC Utilization (MPCU) (Thompson et al., 1991), Innovation Dif- fusion Theory (IDT) (Rogers, 1995), and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) (Bandura, 1986). According to the UTAUT model, behavioral intentions and usage behaviors can influenced by performance expectations, effort expectations, social influences, and facilitation. In addition, the model has been widely used to assess user accept- ance of technology-based learning media, such as YouTube (Guillén-Gámez et al., 2024), Interactive Whiteboard (Wong et  al., 2013), Micro-Lecture (Wijaya et  al., 2022a), online learning (Qiao et al., 2021), and e-learning (Abbad, [2021)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education). The UTAUT-2 model (Fig. [1)](#23-unified-theory-ofacceptance-anduse-oftechnology) proposed by (Venkatesh et al., 2012) extends the applicability and explanatory power of the UTAUT model. In addition, it has three new variables, namely hedonic motivation, price value, and habit. Several stud- ies also showed that it could provide a powerful framework for analyzing people’s adoption of technology. The model has been applied to a variety of fields, such as sociology (Azman Ong et al., 2023), management science (Ramírez-Correa et al., 2019), medical science (Wang et al., 2021), and pedagogy (Alhwaiti, [2023;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Wang et al., 2022).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1** UTAUT-2 model (based on (Venkatesh et al., 2012))

Based on these results, the UTAUT-2 model was used to analyze mathemat- ics teachers’ behavioral intention and use behavior of digital resources. However, price value was not included in this study because teachers’ use of digital resources did not generally take into account the effect of price (Zhou et al., 2022). Previ- ous reports have shown that the ability of the UTAUT model to predict technol- ogy acceptance can be improved by increasing the number of external variables (Ogegbo et al., 2024). Considering that teachers’ ability to integrate technology in this process was a factor that cannot be ignored (Ling Koh et al., 2014), TPACK was included as a variable. The specific variables are described below:

#### 2.3.1 Performance Expectancy (PE)

PE is defined as “the degree to which an individual believes that new technology helps to improve their job performance” (Venkatesh et al., 2003) (p. 447). Previ- ous studies consistently demonstrate the statistically significant impact of PE on user behavioral intention (Arain et al., [2019;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Arpaci et al., [2022;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Graham et al., 2020; Wijaya et al., 2022a). For example, (Guillén-Gámez et al., 2024) used the UTAUT model to investigate teachers’ use of digital competence and its corollaries. In addi- tion, the results showed a correlation between performance expectations and behav- ioral intention. In this study, PE was operationalized as the extent to which teachers believed that using digital resources enhanced their performance in TMC. Conse- quently, the initial hypothesis was that PE was related to behavioral intention:

**Hypothesis 1 (H1).** Teachers’ PE significantly influences their behavioral inten- tion of using digital resources to TMC.

#### 2.3.2 Effort Expectancy (EE)

EE is referred to as “the extent of ease associated with the use of a new technol- ogy” (Venkatesh et al., 2003) (p. 450). EE constitutes a crucial aspect of the UTAUT model and is frequently used in investigations of users’ intention to adopt new tech- nologies (Almagrashi et al., [2023;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Fitrianie et al., 2021). In this study, EE refers to the level of teachers’ effort to use digital resources in TMC. Building upon the role of EE in UTAUT, this study proposes that EE is related to teachers’ behavioral intentions:

**Hypothesis 2 (H2).** Teachers’ EE significantly influences their behavioral inten- tion of using digital resources to TMC.

#### 2.3.3 Social influence (SI)

SI is described as “the level to which individuals perceive that others believe in the use of new technologies” (Venkatesh et al., 2003) (p. 451). SI is recognized as a sig- nificant factor in the Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) (Venkatesh et al., 2003). In this study, SI pertains to the perceptions of mathematics teachers’ colleagues, principals, and students regarding their use of digital resources; this understanding led to the hypothesis that SI was related to behavioral intention:

**Hypothesis 3 (H3).** SI has a positive relationship with teachers’ behavioral inten- tions to use digital resources for TMC.

#### 2.3.4 Facilitating Conditions (FC)

FC are interpreted as “the degree to which individuals believe that organizational and technical infrastructures exist to support the use of new technologies” (Venkatesh et al., 2003) (p. 453). The original UTAUT model assumed that FC only influenced users’ behavior toward new technologies (Venkatesh et  al., 2003). However, the revised UTAUT-2 model suggested that FC not only impacted usage behavior but also influenced users’ behavioral intention (Venkatesh et al., 2012). Previous empiri- cal studies have confirmed that it had a significant positive effect on users’ behavioral intention and usage behavior (Alowayr, [2022;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Wijaya & Weinhandl, 2022). Based on these results, factors, such as accessibility of digital resources, equipment, and tech- nological support can impact mathematics teachers’ intention and actual behavior in using digital resources:

**Hypothesis 4 (H4).** FC has a positive relationship with teachers’ behavioral intentions to use digital resources for TMC.

**Hypothesis 5 (H5).** FC has a positive relationship with teachers continued use of digital resources for TMC.

#### 2.3.5 Hedonic Motivation (HM)

Individuals’ enjoyment and pleasure derived from using technology are defined as HM (Venkatesh et al., 2012), which has been proven to be a key predictive factor in determining technology acceptance and usage (Brown & Venkatesh, 2005). When users perceive a high level of enjoyment and pleasure in using new technologies, it reinforces their behavioral intention (Zhou et al., 2022). In this study, mathemat- ics teachers accessed the internet through digital resources and retrieved relevant resources from databases, which was a new psychological experience for both teach- ers and students in TMC, potentially leading to enjoyment in using technologies. Therefore, using digital resources in teaching activities can bring about feelings of happiness and satisfaction:

**Hypothesis 6 (H6).** Teachers’ HM significantly affects their behavioral intention of using digital resources to TMC.

#### 2.3.6 Habit (HA)

HA is defined as the extent to which individuals tend to perform behavior automati- cally due to learning (Limayem et al., 2007). Verplanken et al. proposed that HA is a memory-based tendency to automatically respond to cues leading to past behavioral performance (Verplanken & Sui, 2019). This cue-response association is acquired through repeated responses to cues in stable environments. HA, as an additional variable in the UTAUT-2 model, not only significantly influences users’ behavio- ral intention to use new technologies but also actively facilitates usage behavior (Venkatesh et al., 2012). These results are in line with several empirical studies who obtained similar results (Dahri et al., 2021; García-Murillo et al., 2023). With the development of digital resources in the field of education, teachers have become accustomed to using the materials for teaching and learning in mathematics class- rooms (Trouche et al., 2020). Therefore, the initial hypothesis was that HA were related to behavioral intention and use behavior:

**Hypothesis 7 (H7).** Teachers’ HA significantly affects their behavioral intention of using digital resources to TMC.

**Hypothesis 8 (H8).** Teachers’ HA significantly affects their use behavior in using digital resources for TMC.

#### 2.3.7 Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)

TPACK was proposed by (Koehler & Mishra, 2005) building upon Shulman’s con- cept of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) (Shulman, 1986). The TPACK framework comprises three core elements: Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogi- cal Knowledge (PK), and Technological Knowledge (TK); and four composite ele- ments: Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Content Knowledge (TCK), Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK), and Technological Pedagogi- cal Content Knowledge (TPACK) (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). There is a consensus that studies on TPACK often facilitate the enhancement of teachers’ abilities to mas- ter and use information technologies (Tang et al., 2023; Yildiz & Arpaci, 2024). Therefore, this study incorporates the TPACK variable into the UTAUT model to examine its association with usage behavior:

**Hypothesis 9 (H9).** Teachers’ TPACK significantly affects their use behavior in using digital resources for TMC.

#### 2.3.8 Behavioral intention to use digital resources

Behavioral intention (BI) is defined as an individual’s willingness to adopt and use technology in the future (Venkatesh et al., 2003), which is one of the most direct fac- tors influencing technology usage behavior (Ting & Yanhong, 2012). In this study, it is defined as the willingness of mathematics teachers to use digital resources. The frequency of mathematics teachers’ usage of digital resources serves as the ultimate dependent variable, such as their utilization of multimedia courseware, micro-vid- eos, and subject software. Therefore, the following hypothesis is proposed:

**Hypothesis 10 (H10).** Teachers’ BI significantly affects their use behavior in using digital resources for TMC.

### 2.4 Research model

This study investigates eight variables based on the UTAUT-2 model, incorporating teachers’ TPACK as an observational variable, resulting in a total of nine variables. These variables can be categorized into three groups as follows:

1. _Independent variables_: PE, EE, SI, FC, HM, HA, and TPACK
2. _Intermediate variables_: BI
3. _Dependent variables_: UB

According to the UTAUT-2 model proposed by (Venkatesh et al., 2012), seven independent variables influence teachers’ use of digital resources in mathemati- cal cultural teaching. These variables, along with one mediating variable and one dependent variable, are integrated to demonstrate their relationships. Figure [2 ](#24-research-model)illus- trates these relationships.

## 3 Materials and methods

This study employed quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional methods to gather data. utilizing the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS- SEM) approach to analyze complex causal models that influence teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC. Additionally, we drew upon the UTAUT-2 model and its associated scales to assess teachers’ intentions and behaviors regarding the use of digital resources in TMC. The surveyed area was located in the central and western 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2** Proposed research model based on the UTAUT-2 model regions of China, characterized by relatively low levels of economic, technological, and educational development (Xu et al., 2021). Investigating these areas provides valuable insights and guidance for enhancing the high-quality and balanced devel- opment of education in underdeveloped regions. A survey questionnaire was dis- tributed online through the professional data survey platform “Wenjuanxing” ([www. wjx. cn)](http://www.wjx.cn), with data collection conducted from January to March 2024. Wenjuanxing was an authoritative online data survey website, that allowed respondents to partici- pate without constraints of time, space, or location. Informed consent and teachers’ survey permissions were obtained from the respondents before distributing the sur- vey questionnaire, and assurances of questionnaire anonymity and data confidential- ity were provided.

### 3.1 Measurement instrument

The survey questionnaire comprised 2 main sections that included (1) demographic information of the respondents, including gender, age, teaching experience, edu- cational background, teaching proficiency, and digital teaching proficiency; (2) an extended version of the UTAUT-2 questionnaire to determine the behavioral inten- tion and actual use of mathematics teachers in using digital resources, and this sec- tion included 9 core variables. These items were adapted from previously validated scales and modified according to the theme of this survey with input from experts. The items underwent standard back-translation procedures (Brislin, 1970), with one investigator translating into Chinese, and another translating back into English to ensure consistency. Following the compilation of the questionnaire, testing was conducted by 2 PhDs, and based on their feedback, some items were modified to enhance readability. Information about the final items used in this study and their references is provided in the Supplementary Material. To mitigate respondent bias towards neutral items and elicit finer distinctions in their attitudes (Wang et  al., 2024), a 6-point Likert scale was used for all items in the second section of the questionnaire. The first eight variables were rated from “1 = completely disagree” to “6 = completely agree”, while the ninth variable, use behavior, was rated from “1 = not used” to “6 = frequently used”. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for this measurement tool was 0.967, indicating high overall reliability.

### 3.2 Participants

The participants in the survey were selected as mathematics teachers, targeting 3 provinces in the central and western regions of China. Surveys were conducted in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Henan Province, and Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with each province receiving 150 questionnaires, totaling 450. After excluding questionnaires with response times of less than 100  s and those exhibiting regular patterns, 418 valid questionnaires remained, resulting in an effec- tive rate of 92.9%. According to (Gorusch, 1983) (pp. 6–9), the observed sample size (S) is related to the number of measurement items (V), where S = V(V-1)/2. Following this principle, considering 9 core variables and a total of 27 measurement items, the sample size should not be less than 351, and the effective sample met the requirements for data analysis, as shown in Table [1.](#33-data-analysis) The demographic character- istics data distribution of this questionnaire was reasonable and suitable for subse- quent analysis stages.

### 3.3 Data analysis

The data analysis was conducted using SPSS 26.0 software and SmartPLS 3.0 software, and this included the following, (1) Descriptive statistical analysis of the respondents’ data was performed using SPSS 26.0 software. (2) Evaluation of the model’s reliability, validity, and effects between variables was carried out using SmartPLS 3.0 software. (3) The PLS-SEM technique was used to elucidate and test the report hypotheses proposed based on the structural model of the study (Anderson & Gerbing, [1988)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education).

Mediation analysis was carried out to examine the mediating role of behavioral intention in the relationship between significant determinants of behavioral intention and usage behavior (Nitzl et al., 2016). This study proposed that it mediated between early and later variables in the causal chain (Fitrianie et al., 2021). For instance, the

This suggested that the majority of teachers believed that using digital resources could enhance the teaching practice of mathematics culture. From the perspective of the mean dimension (PE = 4.839, EE = 5.152, SI = 5.115, FC = 4.813, HM = 4.827, HA = 4.968, TPACK = 5.079, BI = 4.856, UB = 4.945), it was evident that the major- ity of teachers provided positive responses. The average scores for BI and UB were 4.856 and 4.945 respectively, showing their optimistic attitudes towards the inten- tion and behavior of using digital resources. Additionally, the skewness statistics were all lower than \|0.803\|, and the kurtosis statistics were all lower than \|1.499\|. The critical values for skewness and kurtosis, \|2.3\|, were used to assess whether the data were normally distributed or not (Lei & Lomax, 2005). The results showed that both values were within acceptable ranges, suggesting a normal distribution of the data. Therefore, using SEM to analyze the relationships between the structures was appropriate.

### 4.2 Evaluation of the measurement model

The first step in the evaluation of the measurement model was to assess the level to which the variance of each indicator was explained by its structure, represent- ing indicator reliability, and this study reflected the commonality of an indicator. Consequently, indicator loadings above 0.708 were recommended, as such values showed that the construct explained more than 50 percent of the variance, ensuring acceptable reliability (Hair et al., 2021) (p. 77). According to Fig. [3,](#43-evaluation-ofthestructural-model-andhypothesis-testing) the loading fac- tors for the 9 variables (outer model) ranged from 0.789 to 0.911, suggesting that the observed variables must sufficiently explain the latent variables.

Table [3 ](#431-hypothesis-testing)contained information regarding the indicators of the 9 latent variables in the measurement model, such as loading, t-value, Cronbach’s alpha, and composite reliability.

The second step in evaluating the measurement model involved examining its validity, primarily focusing on (1) item reliability, (2) composite reliability, and 

3. Average Variance Extracted (AVE). Regarding item reliability, the Cronbach’s alpha for each latent variable in Table [3 ](#431-hypothesis-testing)ranged from 0.772 to 0.889, all exceeding the threshold limit of 0.70. Next, both convergent validity and discriminant valid- ity using the recommendations of (Hair et al., 2009) and (Fornell & Larcker, 1981) were computed. For convergent validity, (Hair et al., 2009) suggested ensuring both composite reliability (CR ≥ 0.70) and AVE ≥ 0.50. However, for discriminant valid- ity, (Fornell & Larcker, 1981) required that the square root of AVE for each latent variable, such as PE, EE, SI, etc., must exceed the correlations between that vari- able and all other variables. Table [4 ](#432-path-analysis)shows that all scores for convergent validity and discriminant validity exceeded the required thresholds and indicators for testing the report model.

When 2 or more indicators in the measurement model were highly correlated, multicollinearity occurred (Hair et al., 2021) (p. 93). Conducting multicollinearity tests in regression analysis could help eliminate observed reverse effects between independent variables (Zhou et  al., 2022). One aspect of assessing indicator

multicollinearity was the variance inflation factor (VIF), where higher VIF values showed a greater degree of multicollinearity, and VIF values of 5 or above suggested multicollinearity issues (Hair et al., 2021) (p. 96). As shown in Table [5,](#432-path-analysis) none of the latent variables in the model exhibited strong multicollinearity (VIF \< 5), showing the following results, (1) There was no overlap among the items of the 7 constructs, 

2. The items contained within the variables reflected the indicators being measured, and (3) The questionnaire design was reasonable.

### 4.3 Evaluation of the structural model and hypothesis testing

The reliability and validity of the constructed measures were confirmed, and the next step involved evaluating the structural model by calculating the coefficient of determination (R2), SRMR, path coefficients, and effect sizes (Hair et  al., 2021). This evaluation could be conducted using Smart-PLS 3.0 software, using the PLS algorithm with a subsample of 5000, a two-tailed test, and bootstrapping with a sig- nificance level of 5% (Latan & Noonan, 2017). #### 4.3.3 Direct, indirect, and total effects

Based on Table [7 ](#5-discussion-andimplication)the direct, indirect, and total effects of each variable on teachers’ behavioral intention and usage behavior of digital resources in mathematical culture teaching were summarized.

According to the results, it could be observed that the 2 most significant deter- minants affecting behavioral intention were habit and PE, with total effect values of 0.305 and 0.241, respectively. Similarly, the 2 primary factors influencing usage behavior were habit and FC, with total effect values of 0.363 and 0.345, respectively. Teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources significantly influenced their usage behavior, with an effect size of 0.260.

## 5 Discussion and implication

### This study used the UTAUT-2 model in combination with the TPACK factor to explore the factors that influenced teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC, which was an understudied area worldwide. Exploring teachers’ intention to use digital 

resources was crucial because the ability to integrate digital resources into the edu- cational process depended on teachers’ beliefs (Muhaimin et al., 2020). When teach- ers realized the value of using digital resources, educators were more likely to incor- porate these tools into the mathematics classroom. Reports showed that factors such as PE, EE, SI, FC, HM, HA, and TPACK had an explanatory power of 72.4% and 79.3% for behavioral intention and use behavior, respectively, demonstrating the robust explanatory power of our model. Moreover, behavioral intention, serving as a mediating variable, significantly facilitated mathematics teachers’ adoption of digi- tal resources.

### 5.1 Variables that have a significant effect on behavioral intention

According to the results of the study, 4 groups of variables PE, SI, HM, and HA sig- nificantly influenced teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources for TMC, and the most influential factor is HA. This variable had a significant positive effect on teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources for TMC. This implied that teachers’ intention (willingness) to use digital resources was largely influenced by the habit criterion because repeated behaviors, such as the use of digital resources for retrieving instructional materials in preparing instructional designs, increased teachers’ use in the classroom or other settings (Wong et al., 2020). This result was consistent with other investigators (Nikolopoulou et al., 2021; Taamneh et al., 2023) that habit was a significant predictor of behavioral intention.

This was followed by PE, a variable that showed a significant facilitating effect on teachers’ intention to use digital resources. This was consistent with the results of previous related empirical studies (García-Murillo et al., 2023; Wijaya et al., 2022a; Yildiz & Arpaci, 2024), showing that the higher the teachers’ usefulness and expec- tation of digital resources, the more it increased the teachers’ behavioral intention to incorporate digital resources into their TMC.

The third factor, SI, which was also an important indicator of teachers’ willing- ness to use digital resources consistently, was related to the people and environ- ment around teachers. Mathematics teachers believed that the opinions of those who directly influenced their behavioral intentions (e.g., leaders, colleagues, students, parents, etc.) could directly influence their thoughts and intentions. This was consist- ent with the hypotheses and results of previous studies (Teo et al., 2019; Venkatesh et al., 2003), where social influences were positively related to teachers’ willingness to consistently use digital resources for TMC.

Lastly, HM, whose effect on teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources was confirmed in keeping with most of the results (Nikolopoulou et al., 2021; Omar et al., 2019), when teachers perceived the use of digital resources as an enjoyable teaching and learning experience, educators further increased the likelihood of using digital resources in their TMC.

After identifying the four variables that significantly influence teachers’ behavio- ral intentions to use digital resources for TMC, we will now explore how these vari- ables interact in various contexts and impact teachers’ behavioral intentions. First, HA, identified as the most influential factor, is often linked to teachers’ consistent 

use of digital resources in their daily teaching practices. Teachers are more likely to cultivate the habit of using digital resources in environments where technical sup- port is readily available and accessible. Research indicates that establishing positive habits can mitigate resistance to adopting new technologies (Verplanken & Aarts, 1999). Second, teachers are likely to perceive digital resources as more effective and useful when the technological environment is conducive and the resources align closely with pedagogical goals, thereby enhancing the role of PE. For instance, resources that offer an excellent user experience and demonstrate clear pedagogical outcomes can further bolster teachers’ PE. Moreover, the impact of SI may differ across cultural and organizational contexts. In school environments that foster col- laboration and technological innovation, teachers are more likely to be positively influenced by their colleagues and administration to adopt digital resources. Con- versely, in conservative or less technologically receptive settings, SI may have a limited impact on behavioral intentions (Venkatesh et al., 2003). Finally, in envi- ronments rich in interactive and engaging digital resources, teachers’ behavioral intentions to use these tools are likely to be significantly enhanced. By facilitating enjoyable learning experiences, teachers are more inclined to explore and utilize these resources effectively.

Based on the above conclusions, to accelerate the integration of digital resources and education and to increase teachers’ intention to use digital resources in TMC, the following insights were obtained: (1) The school level needed to provide teach- ers with the conditions for using digital resources, and at the same time, set up indicators such as point rewards and teaching evaluation to cultivate the habit of teachers’ use of digital resources by increasing the chances of teachers’ exposure to digital resources. (2) Increase the publicity of digital resources to increase teachers’ expectations of digital resources. (3) Create a favorable atmosphere for using digital resources through peer support or obtaining leadership support to increase teach- ers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources. (4) Institutions or companies could help teachers increase their intention to use digital resources by developing digital educational resources that are easy to use in the classroom to increase the fun and enjoyment of teaching with digital resources.

### 5.2 Variables that have a significant effect on usage behavior

Behavioral intention, as a mediating variable, significantly influenced teachers’ behaviors toward the use of digital resources. This was consistent with the results of empirical studies using the UTAUT model (Arpaci et al., [2022;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Chávez Herting et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). PE, SI, HM, and HA indirectly influenced teachers’ usage behavior in using digital resources for TMC by influencing teachers’ behavio- ral intentions.

FC significantly promoted teachers’ behavior in using digital resources for TMC, although this variable did not have a significant effect on teachers’ behavioral intention, and the results proved that teachers used digital resources in TMC when adequate social support was provided. This result was consistent with the study of (Yuan et al., 2023) that FC tends to increase teachers’ use of digital resources.

HA not only influenced teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources for TMC but also significantly contributed to their actual use behavior. According to (Verplanken & Orbell, 2022), behavior changes with attitude, and in this study, teachers’ attitudes toward the use of digital resources in TMC influenced whether or not the educators adopted the tool for teaching.

TPACK, as a necessary competency for modern teachers (Açıkgül & Aslaner, [2020)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education), had a significant impact on teachers’ behavior in using digital resources. According to previous studies (Schmid et al., 2021; Seufert et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2023), TPACK also had a significant impact on teachers’ digital teaching behaviors. Therefore, this study concluded that one of the important ways to improve teachers’ use behaviors with digital resources was to improve teachers’ TPACK. The interactions among these variables within diverse environments create a complex ecosystem. It is essential to not only examine the mechanisms of these variables but also integrate them with environmental influences to conduct a com- prehensive analysis of the behaviors affecting teachers’ use of digital resources. For instance, a positive school culture, sufficient technical support, and effective train- ing can enhance teachers’ behavioral intention, FC, HA, and TPACK, subsequently improving their usage behavior toward digital resources. Conversely, negative envi- ronmental factors can create barriers for teachers, thereby limiting their potential to effectively use digital resources. Therefore, policymakers and educational lead- ers must consider the interrelationships among these variables when implementing educational technology to foster a supportive environment for teachers’ use of digi- tal resources. Future research should further investigate the dynamic relationships among these factors to optimize the effectiveness of digital resource usage. Based on the above results, to improve teachers’ behavior in using digital resources, attention could be directed towards the following aspects: (1) Focusing on teachers’ behavioral intention to use digital resources, which was an important observational variable of teachers’ digital classroom teaching (Wijaya et al., 2022b). 

2. Schools and society provided teachers with digital teaching support, for example, in China, efforts were made to bolster the construction of information technology infrastructures for teaching in the central and western regions to ensure teachers had access to ample digital teaching resources. (3) Teachers could consciously cultivate the habit of using digital resources, and good habits promoted the sustainable devel- opment of digital classroom teaching. (4) Strengthened the development of teach- ers’ TPACK competence and enhanced their TPACK self-efficacy beliefs (Açıkgül & Aslaner, [2020)](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education).

### 5.3 EE and FC predictors had no significant effect on behavioral intention

EE did not significantly influence teachers’ behavioral intentions to use digital resources for TMC. Limited studies support this finding (Ayaz & Yanartaş, [2020;](#acknowledgements-we-would-like-to-thank-the-graduate-students-research--innovation-fund-of-inner-mongolia-normal-university-cxjjb23024-for-the-support-of-this-studywe-sincerely-thank-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education-for-the-help-proposed-in-our-research-process-this-paper-is-the-result-of-a-major-special-research-project-of-the-henan-provincial-collaborative-innovation-center-for-intelligent-education) Verkijika, 2018). Various perspectives can explain this outcome. One possibility is that EE may not be a crucial factor in shaping teachers’ intentions in this con- text. For instance, self-efficacy may significantly impact these intentions. (Bandura, 1997) defines self-efficacy as an individual’s belief in their ability to perform a task, and research indicates that teachers with high self-efficacy are more likely to adopt new technologies, even when the perceived ease of use is low (Tschannen-Moran & Hoy, 2001). Teachers’ attitudes and trust may play an even more critical role in digital resource use, and the UTAUT model of (Venkatesh et al., 2003) suggests that attitudes and subjective norms are more influential on behavioral intentions than EE. Teachers with positive attitudes towards digital resources may be willing to explore these tools despite low EE. Moreover, the availability of digital resources and cur- riculum design can significantly affect teachers’ intentions, largely independent of EE. According to (Wijaya et al., 2024), many educators today, particularly in China, are digital natives who have engaged with technology from a young age. This famili- arity likely enhances their comfort and proficiency with new technologies, diminish- ing the impact of usability on their intentions.

FC did not significantly affect teachers’ behavioral intentions to use digital resources for TMC, yet they played a crucial role in actual usage behavior. These finding warrants exploration from several perspectives. First, FC encompasses the availability of support and resources, including training, technical assistance, and access to hardware and software. While FC may not directly alter teachers’ behav- ioral intentions, it provides essential support during actual use, thereby influencing their usage behavior. This aligns with the UTAUT model proposed by (Venkatesh et al., 2003), which asserts that FC has a significant direct effect on technology use. Second, teachers’ behavioral intentions are often shaped by psychological factors, whereas FC represents external environmental components. Teachers may experi- ence stress or a lack of confidence when engaging with technology, resulting in weak intentions even in the presence of robust FC. (Ertmer, 1999) notes that teachers may hesitate to adopt new technologies due to insufficient attitude or self-efficacy, even when supportive conditions exist. Finally, the significance of FC in actual use can be understood through the pervasive nature of technology and the complexities of teachers’ daily practices. Even if teachers’ attitudes and intentions regarding digital resources are not overwhelmingly positive, effective FC can provide essential guid- ance and support to help them navigate practical challenges. This phenomenon is corroborated by research in educational technology (Kirkpatrick, 1998), highlight- ing the critical role of FC in facilitating teachers’ practical use of technology. Based on this situation, the following explanations were identified: (1) the ease- of-use factor was not sufficient to increase teachers’ willingness to use digital resources, and (2) based on the adequate infrastructure and related training, teachers were more willing to use digital resources in TMC.

## 6 Limitations and future research

This study filled the gap of influencing factors on teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC, and solid conclusions were obtained through quantitative studies. Unfor- tunately, there were some limitations of this study, which could be seen as a direc- tion for future reports. (1) The sample of this study was from central and western China, and the factors affecting teachers’ use of digital resources could vary in other regions due to cultural differences. We hope that the findings of this study will provide valuable insights for similar regions and countries to enhance educa- tional high-quality and balance through the integration of digital resources in math- ematical education. In the future, we aim to conduct research with a larger sample to compare teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC across different regions and countries.

2. This study examines the factors influencing teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC through the lens of the UTAUT-2 model. Notably, moderating variables such as gender and age may impact the understanding of teachers’ behavioral inten- tions and usage behaviors (Venkatesh et al., 2012). It is suggested that merging these moderating variables could yield new constructs suitable for diverse learning envi- ronments. Consequently, future research should incorporate these variables to inves- tigate their specific roles in teachers’ technology use, ultimately aiding in the design of targeted training and support strategies for different demographics to enhance the effective use of digital resources.
3. This study revealed that behavioral intentions not only directly affect teach- ers’ usage behavior towards digital resources, but also play a mediating role. Future research could further explore this variable by incorporating external factors, such as self-efficacy, attitudes, and subjective norms. This approach may refine and enrich the UTAUT-2 model, deepening our understanding of the influences on mathemat- ics teachers’ use of digital resources for TMC.

## 7 Conclusions

In conclusion, to modernize education, governments, and school programs must prioritize enhancing the integration of digital resources into mathematics teaching activities, specifically in economically, technologically, and educationally underde- veloped regions. This study used the UTAUT-2 model to explore the factors influ- encing mathematics teachers’ behavioral intention and use behavior regarding digi- tal resources for TMC. Among the 10 hypotheses proposed, only EE and FC did not significantly affect behavioral intention, while all other factors showed signifi- cant effects. Notably, teachers’ intentions to use digital resources relied heavily on habitus and performance expectations, while social influence and HM had also been shown to have a significant positive impact. These 4 factors could be targeted to focus on when considering teachers’ intentions to use digital resources. More impor- tantly, facilitation and habitus showed a strong linear relationship with teachers’ use of digital resources, while behavioral intention and TPACK were also found to be significant factors of influence.

The above conclusions were important references for the government, society, and schools in promoting the era of digital teaching and achieving balanced devel- opment of education. In addition, it promoted the construction of digital education infrastructure in underdeveloped areas, cultivated teachers’ habit of using digital education resources, improved teachers’ intention to use mathematical resources, and actively promoted the modernization of education to achieve the sustainable development of education.
